lessons.title: What It Means That Rust Is Compiled
lessons.objective: Explain how running a Rust program differs from running a Python script, and when errors are caught.
lessons.hook: Rust stops many bugs before your program ever runs. That changes how you write and debug code.
lessons.explain: Python reads and runs your source each time you launch it. Rust is compiled: the compiler translates your source into a standalone binary before it runs. The compiler checks your whole program before it runs, so many bugs become compile errors instead of runtime crashes. Example: in Python, len(5) fails only when that line executes. In Rust, passing a number where text is expected stops the build. The binary runs without the Rust compiler installed on the target machine.
key_facts: Rust is compiled: the compiler translates your source into a standalone binary before it runs.
The compiler checks your whole program before it runs, so many bugs become compile errors instead of runtime crashes.
The binary runs without the Rust compiler installed on the target machine.

predict.q: You misspell a function name inside a branch that rarely runs. In Rust, when do you find out?

angles: A translator rewrites a whole book before anyone reads it. An interpreter whispers a speech line by line as it is given. Which of the two notices a contradiction on page 300 before the audience arrives? Which one matches Rust?
Think of a recipe checked by an editor before printing, versus one you discover is wrong halfway through cooking. Decide which kind of mistake Rust is designed to surface, and at what moment.
claims: Rust is a compiled language.

items.why: The compiler checks the whole program before it runs.

lessons.title: Your First Project with Cargo
lessons.objective: Create, build and run a Rust project with Cargo, and identify fn main and the println! macro.
lessons.hook: Cargo is how every real Rust project is built, tested and shipped.
lessons.aside: Cargo.toml plays roughly the role that pyproject.toml plays in modern Python projects: it holds the project metadata and dependencies.
lessons.explain: Cargo is Rust's build tool and package manager. It fetches dependencies, as pip does, and it also builds and runs your project. `cargo new hello` creates a project with Cargo.toml and src/main.rs. Every Rust program starts executing in fn main. `cargo run` compiles the project and then runs the binary. Example: src/main.rs contains fn main() { println!("Hello"); }. The ! in println! marks it as a macro, not a function. Unlike Python, there is no top-level code that runs on its own.

lessons.title: Immutable by Default: let, mut and Shadowing
lessons.objective: Declare immutable and mutable variables, and choose between mut and shadowing.
lessons.hook: Rust makes you say when a value can change. Mutation stops being a surprise.
lessons.explain: In Python, any name can be rebound. In Rust, variables declared with let are immutable by default. Adding mut makes a variable changeable. Example: let x = 5; x = 6; fails to compile, but let mut x = 5; x = 6; works. Shadowing means declaring a new variable with the same name using let again. For instance, let x = 5; let x = x + 1; creates a new x equal to 6. Shadowing can change the type, while mut cannot.
key_facts: variables declared with let are immutable by default.
Adding mut makes a variable changeable.
Shadowing means declaring a new variable with the same name using let again
Shadowing can change the type, while mut cannot.

items.answer: Shadowing, e.g. let input: i32 = input.parse().unwrap(); because shadowing can change the type and mut cannot.
accept: Shadow it with a new let, since the type changes from text to a number.
items.why: Going from text to a number is a type change, which only shadowing allows.

lessons.title: Static Types and Type Inference
lessons.objective: Predict variable types, recognise default numeric types, and convert between numeric types explicitly.
lessons.hook: Knowing the type rules turns most compile errors from mysteries into quick fixes.
lessons.explain: Rust is statically typed: every variable's type is fixed at compile time. Python, by contrast, checks types only as code runs. Type inference lets the compiler work out types, so you rarely write them. An integer literal with no other hint defaults to i32, and a float defaults to f64. Example: let n = 3; is an i32, while let price: f64 = 9.5; is annotated. Mixing types needs explicit conversion: n as f64 + price works, but n + price does not compile.

lessons.title: Ownership: Who Frees the Memory
lessons.objective: State the ownership rules and predict when a value is dropped.
lessons.hook: Ownership is how Rust stays memory-safe without a garbage collector. Everything else builds on it.
lessons.aside: Python's main mechanism is reference counting. It adds a cycle-detecting collector for reference cycles.
lessons.explain: Python frees memory at runtime, using reference counting and a garbage collector. Rust has no garbage collector; ownership rules decide when memory is freed, checked at compile time. Each value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed. Example: { let s = String::from("hi"); }. At the closing brace, s goes out of scope and the String is dropped. A String stores its text on the heap, and that heap memory is released on drop.
key_facts: Rust has no garbage collector; ownership rules decide when memory is freed, checked at compile time.
Each value has exactly one owner.
When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped and its memory freed.
A String stores its text on the heap
fixes: Expects a runtime garbage collector or reference counting to free memory, as in Python
angles: Think of a library book with a single name written on its card. Nobody tracks it afterwards: the moment that person leaves the building, the book goes back on the shelf by itself. Map the person, the building and the book onto a variable, its block and its value.
Picture a hotel room key tied to one guest. Checkout happens automatically when the guest walks out the front door. Decide what in Rust plays the role of the front door.

lessons.title: Moves: Why Assignment Isn't Sharing
lessons.objective: Predict when assignment or a function call moves a value, and when it copies.
lessons.hook: This is where Python intuition breaks most often. Getting it right removes most early compile errors.
lessons.explain: In Python, b = a makes both names refer to the same object. In Rust, let b = a; with a String moves ownership to b, and a can no longer be used. Using a after the move is a compile error (E0382). Passing a String to a function also moves it. Simple types like i32, bool and f64 implement Copy, so assignment copies them and both stay usable. Example: after let x = 5; let y = x; the variable x is still usable.
key_facts: let b = a; with a String moves ownership to b, and a can no longer be used.
Using a after the move is a compile error
Passing a String to a function also moves it.
Simple types like i32, bool and f64 implement Copy, so assignment copies them and both stay usable.
fixes: Assumes `let b = a;` makes two names share one value, as Python assignment does

lessons.title: Clone: Making an Independent Copy
lessons.objective: Use .clone() to keep two usable values, and judge its cost.
lessons.hook: Clone is the simplest way out of a move error. Knowing what it costs keeps your code fast.
lessons.explain: When you need two independent copies of a String, call .clone(). let b = a.clone(); duplicates the heap data, so a and b each own their own String and both stay usable. Cloning costs time and memory proportional to the data size. Example: let a = String::from("hi"); let b = a.clone(); println!("{} {}", a, b); prints hi hi. Changing b afterwards does not affect a. Clone is explicit, so expensive copies are visible in the code.
key_facts: let b = a.clone(); duplicates the heap data, so a and b each own their own String and both stay usable.

lessons.title: Borrowing with Shared References
lessons.objective: Pass values by shared reference so the caller keeps ownership, and know what a &T allows.
lessons.hook: Borrowing lets functions use your data without taking it. Most real Rust functions take references.
lessons.explain: Moving a value into a function loses it; borrowing avoids that. &a creates a reference that borrows a without taking ownership. A function taking &String can read the String, and the caller still owns it afterwards. You can have any number of shared references at once. Shared references are read-only: you cannot modify data through a &T. Example: fn len(s: &String) -> usize { s.len() }, called as len(&name), leaves name usable. This resembles a Python name, but the compiler guarantees the reference never outlives the owner.

A function taking &String can read the String, and the caller still owns it afterwards.

lessons.title: Mutable References and the Borrow Rule
lessons.objective: Use &mut to modify borrowed data, and apply the one-mutable-or-many-shared rule.
lessons.hook: This one rule is the heart of the borrow checker. It is why Rust programs avoid data races.
lessons.explain: To change borrowed data, use a mutable reference: &mut a, which requires a to be declared mut. Rust's core borrow rule is this: at any time you can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references, never both. Example: let r1 = &mut s; let r2 = &mut s; followed by a use of r1 fails to compile. In Python, two names can mutate the same list freely. Rust forbids this to prevent data races and iterator invalidation. A borrow ends after its last use, so sequential mutable borrows are fine.
key_facts: use a mutable reference: &mut a, which requires a to be declared mut.
at any time you can have either one mutable reference or any number of shared references, never both.
Rust forbids this to prevent data races and iterator invalidation.
A borrow ends after its last use, so sequential mutable borrows are fine.
fixes: Assumes several names can mutate the same data at once, as with Python lists

items.q: Why does Rust forbid two mutable references to the same data at once?
options: To prevent data races and invalidation
To let the garbage collector run faster
To keep the binary size small
items.answer: To prevent data races and invalidation

items.q: State Rust's core borrowing rule.
items.answer: At any time, either one mutable reference or any number of shared references, never both.
accept: One &mut or many &, but not both at once.
items.why: This is the rule the borrow checker enforces.

items.q: What two things are needed to modify s through a reference?
items.answer: Declare s with let mut, and borrow it with &mut s.
accept: s must be mut, and you take &mut s.
items.why: Mutable borrows require a mutable variable.

lessons.title: Reading and Fixing Borrow Checker Errors
lessons.objective: Diagnose E0382 and E0499 from compiler output and apply the standard fixes.
lessons.hook: In production you'll read compiler errors daily. Fixing them fast is a core Rust skill.
lessons.explain: Reading the borrow checker's errors is a daily skill. Every error has a code like E0382, and you can run rustc --explain E0382 for a full write-up. E0382 means a value was used after being moved; fix it by borrowing with & or by cloning. E0499 means two mutable borrows overlap; fix it by ending the first borrow before starting the second. Example: let t = s; println!("{}", s); triggers E0382. Change it to let t = &s; and it compiles. The error points at both the move and the later use.
key_facts: run rustc --explain E0382 for a full write-up.
E0382 means a value was used after being moved; fix it by borrowing with & or by cloning.
E0499 means two mutable borrows overlap; fix it by ending the first borrow before starting the second.
The error points at both the move and the later use.

angles: Compiler error codes work like fault codes on a dishwasher: the code alone is a lookup key. Consider which tool installed with Rust could expand that key into a long explanation.
Read the error like a delivery log that records where a parcel changed hands. Ask yourself what you could do at that handover so the original is still there when it's needed again.

rungs.text: Error E0382 at println!("{}", s); after let t = s;. Read it: s was moved into t. Fix it: let t = &s;. Rebuild: it compiles.
Error E0499: r1 and r2 are both &mut v, and r1 is used after r2 is created. Read it: two ____ borrows overlap. Fix it: finish using ____ before creating r2.

items.q: What does E0382 output highlight in your code?
options: The move and the later use
Only the line of the later use
items.answer: The move and the later use
items.why: The error points at both the move and the later use.
misconceptions: Only the failing use is shown.
Only the declaration is flagged.
Move errors concern return types.

items.q: How do you fix E0499?
items.answer: End the first mutable borrow before starting the second, e.g. finish using r1 before creating r2.
accept: Make the mutable borrows sequential instead of overlapping.
items.why: A borrow ends after its last use.

items.q: Name two ways to fix E0382.
items.answer: Borrow with & instead of moving, or clone the value.
items.why: Either one keeps the original value usable.
